# ASSUMPTIONS and provisional values

Every unverified value or modelling choice in the pipeline. **"Owner must verify"** = I could not check it against a
primary source offline; check it against your own copy before the report goes to the guide.

Legend: status `provisional` = not verified; `chosen` = a modelling decision (reversible, in a YAML); `sourced` = verified.

## A. IS 456:2000 tables and constants (`config/is456_tables.yaml`) - CHECKED against the printed code on 2026-11-11

All items A1-A11 were compared with the owner's copy `is.456.2000.pdf` (page-by-page record: `docs/IS456_VERIFICATION.md`); no value had to change. Status `sourced`.

Cost *level* is not meaningful until you do; the Pareto *shape* depends on the ratios (steel/concrete) so run the sensitivity page.

## D. Embodied-carbon factors (`config/carbon_factors.yaml`)

Since 2026-10-04 cement (PPC 0.507, OPC 0.92 kgCO2e/kg) and reinforcement (2.5 kgCO2e/kg) use Indian **secondary-source** values (`status: secondary_source`; not EPDs, owner should replace with supplier EPDs).
STILL PROVISIONAL: cement content per grade (360-450 kg/m3), other concrete constituents (12 kgCO2e/m3), A4 transport (30 km concrete, 500 km steel, 0.11 kgCO2e/(t km)). Formwork carbon excluded.
Details and sources: `docs/CARBON_DATA_AUDIT.md`.

## D2. Cement type (design variable, D-028)
Cement prices OPC 7.9 / PPC 7.5 / PSC 7.3 INR/kg (mid of 2026 market-listing ranges, secondary, PROVISIONAL); concrete rates are taken to assume PPC. Cement content per grade is the same for all types (PPC/PSC may need more cement for the same early strength: not modelled). PSC availability in central India is limited: not modelled.

## E. STAAD benchmark (see `docs/BENCHMARK.md`)

OpenSees (benchmark mode) reproduces STAAD's gravity results: reactions and vertical displacements to 0.001 %, column axial forces to 0.003 %,
column moments (> 20 kN.m) to 0.13 %. Two effects were needed and are documented there (wall-load eccentricity torque, shear deformation).
**Not validated by STAAD:** the cracked-stiffness modifiers (0.35 / 0.70), Ec = 5000 sqrt(fck), depth-following wall loads, beam end forces
(STAAD beam design was aborted), anything seismic/wind. Owner must decide whether 0.35 Ig / 0.70 Ig is the stiffness they want to defend.

benchmark_markdown:
# BENCHMARK: OpenSeesPy vs STAAD.Pro (owner's G+3 model)

Generated by `rcopt phase0b` (`src/rcopt/fe/benchmark.py`); gate test: `tests/test_benchmark.py`.

## Setup
* Reference: results already stored in `legacy/staad_model` for the owner's model `G+3 RCC FINAL`
  (120 joints, 255 members, 20 fixed supports): reactions (`.rea`) and joint displacements (`.dsp`) for the 35 load cases,
  and the IS 456 column design report (`.ANL`, 76 columns whose guiding case is 11 = 1.5 (DL + LL)).
  STAAD stores these binaries in kip / inch; conversion verified by the dead-load total (see below).
  **No STAAD licence was used by this project**; the owner's files are only read.
* OpenSees model in **benchmark mode**: STAAD's own material (E = 2.17184e7 kN/m2, density 23.5615 kN/m3, nu 0.17),
  uncracked sections (modifiers 1.0), STAAD's sections (beams 300 x 450, columns 450 x 450), STAAD's fixed wall loads,
  floor loads 4.75 / 5.25 kN/m2 distributed by yield-line tributary areas, live 2.0 / 1.5 kN/m2.
* Design mode (used for the optimisation) differs from benchmark mode only by: E = 5000 sqrt(fck), 25 kN/m3,
  cracked modifiers (0.35 / 0.70) and wall loads that follow the beam depth. Those are pure scalings of E, I and loads;
  STAAD (uncracked) cannot validate them, which is why they are listed in `docs/ASSUMPTIONS.md` (B6) as choices.

## Result (max relative differences, 20 supports / 120 joints / 76 columns)

| Variant | Reaction Fy (DL) | Disp. dy (case 11) | Disp. dx,dz (DL), abs | Column Pu | Column M (>= 20 kN.m): about Z / Y | Column M, all (abs max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Euler-Bernoulli, no wall torque | 1.927 % | 1.905 % | 0.858 mm | 1.891 % | 9.514 % / 8.369 % | 7.84 kN.m |
| B. A + STAAD wall-load eccentricity (d3 = 0.15 m) | 0.149 % | 0.165 % | 0.018 mm | 0.162 % | 0.697 % / 0.722 % | 5.00 kN.m |
| C. B + shear deformation (Timoshenko) = benchmark mode | 0.001 % | 0.001 % | 0.000 mm | 0.003 % | 0.117 % / 0.127 % | 0.10 kN.m |

Dead-load total: STAAD 17580.88 kN, OpenSees 17580.88 kN
(hand total of the model's loads: 17,580 kN). Live-load total: 2850.00 vs 2850.00 kN.

**Verdict: PASS** (targets were forces within 5 %, deflections within 10 %). With variant C every compared quantity agrees to better than
0.2 % (column moments > 20 kN.m) / 0.005 % (reactions, vertical displacements, axial forces); the largest absolute column-moment
difference is 0.10 kN.m.

## What explained the first discrepancies (found, tested, not hidden)
1. **Wall-load eccentricity.** STAAD's `UNI GY -11.73 0 5 0.15` carries a 0.15 m perpendicular offset, which creates a torque on every
   wall-loaded beam. Ignoring it left a 1.9 % reaction error and a 115 % error in the horizontal dead-load displacements (STAAD's
   dead-load sway of up to 0.92 mm, and its asymmetric support reactions, come from this torque). Applying the torque with the offset
   toward the member's local +z (X-beams +Z, Z-beams -X; my reading of STAAD's convention, confirmed by the fit) removes it.
2. **Shear deformation.** STAAD includes it; `elasticBeamColumn` does not. It matters for the 1.0 m stub columns (L/D = 2.2):
   differences of up to ~5 kN.m in stub moments disappeared when the model was switched to `ElasticTimoshenkoBeam`
   (shear area 5/6 A). The design pipeline therefore uses Timoshenko elements too (`solver.yaml: fe.shear_deformation`).

## Limits of this benchmark
* STAAD member end forces for beams are not available (STAAD's beam design was aborted in the `.ANL`, and `.bmd` is undocumented):
  beam moments / shears are validated only through equilibrium (reactions, column forces) and the closed-form tests in `tests/test_fe_sanity.py`.
* Moment units of the `.rea` file were not needed (only forces compared); column moments come from the `.ANL` text in kN.m.
* Gravity cases only (cases 5, 6, 11). Wind / seismic cases were not compared and are out of scope.
* The compared `.ANL` columns are the 76 whose guiding case is 11; the other 57 columns are governed by seismic cases.

## 2. Not verifiable from the printed code (kept, flagged)
* **Fig. 4 / Fig. 5 span-to-depth modification factors** (cl. 23.2.1): the printed standard gives only the curves. The project uses a closed-form fit, **for a diagnostic only** (never a constraint). Owner: read two points off the printed Fig. 4 if you want to quote the diagnostic.
* **Effective length le = 1.2 × unsupported length** (a modelling choice for gravity-only frames; Annex E / Table 28 are not evaluated). See `docs/ASSUMPTIONS.md` B8.

## 3. Where the project is deliberately stricter than the code
1. **Minimum eccentricity about both axes at once.** cl. 25.4 says that for biaxial bending it is sufficient to ensure the eccentricity exceeds the minimum **about one axis at a time**; the project applies it about both axes at the same time (conservative, `docs/ASSUMPTIONS.md` F3).
2. **Deflection after partitions.** cl. 23.2 (b) also limits the deflection that occurs *after* partitions and finishes to span / 350 or 20 mm. The FE model cannot separate that part from the total, so only the total ≤ span / 250 is checked. State this in the report.
3. **Column steel cap of 4 %** instead of the code's 6 % (the code's own note recommends 4 % where bars overlap).

# Carbon data audit (Indian-context availability of embodied-carbon factors)

Scope: A1-A4 of frame materials (concrete, reinforcement). Updated 2026-10-04: the cement and steel factors were replaced by **Indian secondary-source values**
(web research; the ICE spreadsheet and manufacturer EPDs themselves were NOT opened, so these are `status: secondary_source`, not `sourced`). Cement content per grade, the other
concrete constituents and A4 transport are still `provisional`. The gap itself is a finding (Brief s4).

| Factor | Used | Source found (secondary) | India-specific? | Confidence | Gap / action for the owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cement PPC (default) | **0.507 kgCO2e/kg** | India PPC about 507 kg CO2/t cement, i.e. 31 % below OPC ([Indian OPC / blended-cement study](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/376684607_Study_on_energy_use_and_carbon_emission_from_manufacturing_of_OPC_and_blended_cements_in_India), reported via [CEEW](https://www.ceew.in/publications/how-can-india-decarbonise-for-net-zero-cement-industry)) | yes | medium | Replace by the EPD of the cement actually delivered (UltraTech / ACC / Ambuja ...) |
| Cement OPC | 0.92 kgCO2e/kg | India OPC 893-940 kg CO2/t cement over five zones (same study; mid-value) | yes | medium | as above |
| Indian cement-industry average (cross-check) | not used | 0.617-0.68 t CO2/t cement (2020-21), [NITI Aayog cement roadmap](https://niti.gov.in/sites/default/files/2026-01/Roadmap_for_Cement_Sector_Decarbonaisation.pdf) | yes | medium | PPC 0.507 and OPC 0.92 bracket this average, as expected for a blended-cement market |
| Reinforcement (Fe415 = Fe500) | **2.5 kgCO2e/kg** | India steel sector 2.55 tCO2/t crude steel ([CEEW](https://www.ceew.in/publications/how-can-india-decarbonise-for-net-zero-steel-industry)); major producers 2.53 and other producers 2.02 tCO2/t in 2023-24; electric-furnace TMT "over 2" ([Lodha](https://www.lodhagroup.com/blogs/sustainability/rebar-opportunity-decarbonising-backbone-of-india-construction)); scrap-EAF green TMT 0.592 (EPD) | yes | medium | The route (BF-BOF / DRI + induction / scrap-EAF) decides; 2.5 is the Indian average, not the factor of the mill you buy from. Obtain mill EPDs |
| Cement content per grade | 360 / 390 / 420 / 450 kg/m3 (M25-M40) | none found | no | low | Use the ready-mix plant's IS 10262 mix design; this is the main driver of the concrete term |
| Other concrete constituents | 12 kgCO2e/m3 | none found | no | low | aggregates, admixture, batching |
| Resulting concrete (M30, PPC) | about 195 kgCO2e/m3 | consistent with typical Indian ready-mix values quoted at roughly 200-300 kgCO2e/m3 (not verified) | partly | low | |
| A4 transport | 30 km concrete, 500 km steel, 0.11 kgCO2e/(t km) | none found | no | low | actual distances |
| Formwork carbon | excluded | n/a | n/a | n/a | out of scope, flagged |

## Consequences
* With these factors reinforcement carries about 0.036 kgCO2e per INR (2.5 per INR 70) and concrete only about 0.03 kgCO2e per INR (about 195 kgCO2e/m3 for INR 6000/m3, before formwork cost), so carbon is steel-dominated while cost is spread over concrete, formwork and steel. That mismatch is the realistic source of any cost-carbon trade-off (more concrete to save steel). `docs/REPORT_DRAFT.md` reports what the optimiser actually found.
* The cost rates remain provisional placeholders: the width of the front depends on the ratio of cost to carbon per material, so replacing the cost rates can change it as much as the carbon factors.
* Absolute kgCO2e must not be quoted as final until cement content, transport and the actual supplier EPDs replace the remaining assumptions.
